KEY MESSAGE 1...As of 2:40 PM EDT...Broad upper ridge is located 
over the center of the country, with several impulses tracking 
along its northern periphery over the next few days. One of 
those moved through this morning, with another weak impulse back
over the eastern Great Lakes tracking to the southeast over the
next few hours. At the surface, a stationary/warm front is 
located near our southwestern border with BGM across Ulster and 
Dutchess Counties. Near the front, there has been some breaks of
clearing that have allowed 1500-2000 J/kg of SBCAPE to develop 
with steepening mid-level lapse rates. This unstable airmass is
overlapping with 40-45 kt of effective deep-layer shear per the
latest SPC Mesonanalysis. The approaching shortwave impulse, 
low-level front, differential heating along the front, and 
outflow from showers located near/just southwest of I-90 could 
act as lifting mechanisms leading to CI over the next couple of 
hours. 

If/when convection develops, discrete supercells will be possible, 
with the main threats being damaging winds and large hail. An 
isolated tornado can't be ruled out, with the greatest concern where 
flow is more backed in N/S oriented river valleys. SPC has 
maintained a slight risk for southwestern Ulster and Dutchess 
Counties. Greatest threat will exist through early evening, at 
which points convection should move off to the south of our 
area. Locally heavy rainfall will also be possible with any of 
these cells. WPC has maintained the marginal risk ERO today for 
much of our area, although the threat is really limited to just 
the southwestern corner of our CWA, roughly the same as where 
the SPC slight risk is. Highs this afternoon will range from 
around 80 near I-84 to the 60s across northern areas.

Convection should end this evening as sfc high pressure builds in 
from the northeast. Some patchy fog/mist/drizzle will be possible 
overnight with some low-level moisture trapped beneath a developing 
inversion, with lows in the 50s to low 60s.


KEY MESSAGE 2...Tomorrow is now looking relatively dry for our 
region through at least mid to late afternoon. The sfc frontal 
boundary will retreat well south and west of our region tonight with 
no real large-scale forcing through tomorrow as heights aloft 
actually rise through the morning. The sfc high to the E/NE will 
result in low-level cool easterly flow into the region and abundant 
cloud cover, which should help keep temperatures in the 60s 
(terrain) to 70s (valleys). We went a couple degrees below the NBM 
for daytime highs tomorrow. There are some signals that a weakening 
MCS may track south of the region in association with a weak upper 
impulse during the day, but not expecting any impact locally from 
this feature.

Tomorrow evening and night into Thursday, a stronger uper impulse 
will be tracking over the top of the upper ridge, along with an 
associated MCS that is expected to develop over southern Canada. 
Elevated instability looks to increases to 500-1000 J/kg ahead 
of this MCS tomorrow evening into tomorrow night as there are 
some hints of a remnant EML layer tracking overhead. Given this 
and impressive unidirectional deep-layer shear, we are expecting
convection to be able to sustain itself as it tracks across our
region tomorrow night. There doesn't look to be much surface-
based instability, so wind threat actually looks lower than we 
might typically expect. However, large hail will be possible 
with any stronger storms given the elevated instability, 
relatively cool low- levels, and strong deep-layer 
shear/straight hodographs. SPC has maintained the marginal risk 
for severe for western areas tomorrow, but an expansion further 
east is possible over the next 12-24 hrs or so. 

There is also a threat for locally heavy rain leading to flash 
flooding tomorrow evening into Thursday. PWATs remain elevated at 
around 1.8-2.0 inches. The core of the MCS should track through the 
region relatively quickly with fast flow aloft, but along the edges 
of the MCS there is more potential for backbuilding and training, 
and Corfidi upshear vectors are fairly slow at 10-15 kt so this
will have to be watched. WPC has kept the slight risk ERO for 
the western Mohawk Valley and far southern ADKs , with a 
marginal risk for the rest of the region. Rainfall rates of over
1" per hour with total rainfall amounts generally around 0.5 to
1.5", with some locally higher amounts of 2-3" not out of the 
question where any training occurs. So, isolated to possibly 
scattered instances of flash flooding can't be ruled out, 
although potential for main stem river flooding looks very low 
(<10%). With just isolated to possibly scattered flash flood
threat and some uncertainty in exact track of the MCS, did not
feel a flood watch is warranted at this time. 

Thursday forecast remains somewhat nebulous, and will likely depend
